text: Before we go any further into this night, I want to take you somewhere the story does not usually go. Down. Under the streets. Under the houses. Under the lamps and the prayers and the men on the wall. There is a city underneath this city, and almost nobody in it has ever seen the whole of it. Not the emperor. Not the patriarch. Not the general who commands the walls. There are men who know one staircase, one corridor, one flooded room, and have known it their whole lives, and have never once been able to draw you a map. We are going to walk down a hundred and something steps, and stand in the dark, and listen. The first thing you notice is the cold. It comes up the stairs to meet you, the way cold does, like something alive that has been waiting. The second thing you notice is the smell. Wet stone. Not rot. Stone does not rot. It is a clean, mineral smell, old and patient, and it is the smell of a place that has been wet for a thousand years and does not intend to stop. The third thing you notice is that you can hear the city, but only a little. The noise of the street comes down the stairwell thin and far away, the way a voice comes through a wall. Everything else is water. Now. Look up. You are standing in a forest. Not a real forest.

A forest of columns, hundreds of them, rising out of black water, and every one of them is carrying a ceiling you cannot see. Some of them are carved. Some of them are plain. Some of them are not columns at all, in the way a column is supposed to be a column. One of them has a face on it. One of them is standing upside down. They were brought here from somewhere else. That is the thing I want you to hold on to. Every one of these columns used to be part of a temple, or a triumphal arch, or a bath, or a palace that nobody remembers. When this cistern was built, the city was already old, and the builders did what builders have always done. They used what was there. They took the columns down, and rolled them here, and stood them up in the dark, and put a roof on them, and filled the space with water. The temple is gone. The column is still working. There are, in this city, more than a hundred cisterns. Some of them are small enough to be a rich man's cellar. Some of them are the size of a church. There are open cisterns too, great square holes in the ground that the people call by the name of whatever grows in them now, because a thing that holds water in one century holds cabbages in the next. And there is an aqueduct, crossing the middle of the city on arches so tall that a child can walk under them and feel the size of the sky.

It brings water from the hills, from rivers and springs a long way out, along a line of stone that men have been repairing, and repairing, and repairing, since before anyone now alive was born. A city is not only a place where people live. It is a machine for staying alive, and most of that machine is out of sight. You can see the walls. The walls are the part everyone photographs, in the centuries when there are cameras. But the walls are the least interesting part of the machine, because the walls only decide how a city dies. The water decides whether it lives. Let us think about the numbers for a moment, in the way the men who ran this city had to think about them. Nine thousand people. Perhaps a little more. Perhaps a little less. Nobody knows, because nobody has ever counted properly, and on a night like this nobody is going to start. Nine thousand people need water. Not a great deal of it, by the standards of a river. But they need it every day, and they need it to be clean, because a city without water does not simply get thirsty. It gets sick. It gets a fever. It gets the kind of death that moves from house to house without knocking. So there is a rule in this city, and it is older than any emperor, and it is written down nowhere, because everyone knows it. Before a siege, you fill the cisterns. Not when the army appears. Before.

When the rumours start. When the men who sell horses begin to leave. When the price of grain does a thing that grain should not do in a quiet month. You fill them slowly, because water takes time to move, and you fill them quietly, because panic is faster than water. And then you close the lids, and you put a lock on the lid, and you give the key to a man who has been given keys his whole life and has never lost one. Tonight, the cisterns are full. I want you to picture that. Under the streets, under the churches, under the houses where people are trying to sleep, there is a second city made entirely of water. Still. Black. Cold. Holding a month, perhaps two months, of life in the dark. And it is completely silent, except for one sound. The drip. You will hear it before you see anything. It is not a leak. It is not a fault. It is the sound of a full cistern breathing. Water gathers on the ceiling, on the old brick, on the underside of a roof that was laid by men who are now only names on a stone somewhere, and it lets go, and it falls, and it lands. And the sound it makes in a room like this is the most patient sound in the world. The men who check the cisterns come down once a night. There are three of them. One carries the lamp. One carries a long stick with a mark cut into it, a notch at the height the water should be.

One carries nothing at all, and does the counting of the steps, because he has done it so many times that he can tell, by the number of steps, whether they have come down the right stair. They do not talk much. The room does not want them to. Their voices come back at them off the water with a delay, and a man who hears his own voice come back gets quiet very fast. They walk along the edge. The lamp makes a small orange circle on the water and the circle does not stay still, because the water is not still, even when it looks still. It shivers. It has its own small weather. The man with the stick lowers it in. He finds the bottom. He lifts it out. He holds it beside the lamp and looks at the wet line, and he compares the wet line to the notch. And then he says one word, to the other two, and the word is usually the same word, and the word means: enough. Tonight, the word is enough. I like these three men. I like them very much. They are not heroes. Nobody will write about them. If the city survives, they will go back to their ordinary work and nobody will ever ask them what they did on the night of the twenty-eighth of May. But they are the ones who make the rest of the night possible.

Because everything that happens up there, on the wall, in the church, in the streets, in the palace, depends on this: that when a man is thirsty at three in the morning, there is water, and it is close, and he does not have to leave his post to find it. That is what a civilisation is, when you take it apart. Not the gold. Not the crowns. Not the ceremonies. Somebody, somewhere, has arranged for the water to be there. Now let us go a little deeper. There is one more thing down here, and it is the thing that makes this place more than a cellar. Somewhere in the dark, past the columns, past the end of the lamp's reach, there is a wall that is not a wall of this cistern. It is older. It is brick, and it is very thick, and it goes up past where the ceiling should be. It is the foundation of something that used to stand here before the cistern was dug. A temple, perhaps. A house. Nobody is sure. And in the wet brick, at about the height of a man's chest, there is a hole. It is not a big hole. It is the size of two fists. It was made by men, not by water, and it was made recently, because the edges are still sharp. I want to be careful here, because this is the part of the night where the story usually turns into a ghost story, and I do not want to give you a ghost. I want to give you something worse, and better, and much more ordinary.

There are men on the other side of that wall. They are digging. They have been digging for weeks. They are not trying to get into the cistern. They are trying to get under the wall, out there, the great wall, the one with the emperor's name on it, and they are using the old drains and the old foundations as a road, because a road underground is a road nobody is watching. And the men of the city are digging too, from this side, with their ears. That is what the hole is for. They put their faces close to it, and they listen, and they try to work out which way the sound is going, and how far away it is, and whether it is under the wall or under the street or under the church. And when they are sure, they dig their own tunnel, and they fill it with fire, and they light it, and they run. I am not going to describe what happens then. This is not that kind of night, and this is not that kind of channel. But I want you to notice what it means. It means that this siege is not only happening above, where we can see it. It is happening below, in the dark, in the water, in the brick, in the space between two foundations, where two groups of tired men are listening to each other through a wall and trying to guess which of them will be surprised. The man with the lamp does not go near the hole. He has been told not to.

He is not a soldier and he is not a mason and his job is the water. But he hears it, once, as they turn to go back up. A sound through the brick. Not loud. A scrape, and then a pause, and then another scrape. And he stands still for a moment with the lamp in his hand, and the water shivering around his feet, and he thinks a thought that I would like to give him, because it seems to me the most human thought in this whole city. He thinks: they are digging in the dark, too. That is the thing about this night that I keep coming back to. Everyone in it is in the dark. The emperor does not know what the sultan is doing. The sultan does not know what the emperor is doing. The men on the wall do not know what the men under the wall are doing. The men in the boats do not know what the men on the hill are doing. And every one of them is doing the best they can with the little that they can see. Let us go back up. The stairs are steep and there are a hundred and something of them, and by the time you reach the top your legs are burning and the air smells of dust and smoke and the ordinary world. Behind you, the door closes. And under the street, in the dark, the water keeps its level, and the drip keeps its time, and the city keeps its second clock, which nobody winds and nobody stops.

Come with me to the wall. Not the top of it, where the men stand. The bottom. The place where the wall meets the ground, and where, if you look closely, you can see how it was made. Most people look at a wall and see a wall. A flat thing. A thing that stops you. A mason looks at a wall and sees a hundred decisions. This stone came from here. That one came from there. This one is new, cut last year from the quarry beyond the hill. That one is old, much older than the wall, and it has been in three buildings before this one, and if you turn it over you will find a name on it. That is what I want to show you tonight. Not the wall as a barrier. The wall as a library. Here is a block, at about the height of your shoulder, on the inner face, where the mortar has worn away and the stone is showing. Look at the edge. There are letters. They are Greek, and they are old, older than the wall, older than the empire that built the wall. They were cut by a man with a chisel and a steady hand, in a workshop somewhere in this city, for a building that has since fallen down. Perhaps a temple. Perhaps a monument to a charioteer. Perhaps the base of a statue of a man who was important for about eleven years and is now completely forgotten. The stone was cut to fit that building. Then the building went.

Then the stone was carried here, and turned, and set into the wall, and the letters were put face down, or face in, where nobody would have to look at them. Except that the mortar has worn away, and now you are looking at them. There is a word for this, and it is a good word, and it comes from Latin. Spolia. The spoils. The things taken from one place and used in another. The Romans did it. The Byzantines did it. Every city that has ever been built on top of another city has done it, because stone is heavy and men are tired and the cheapest quarry in the world is the building next door that nobody is using anymore. But I do not think it is only economics. I think there is something else in it, and I want to say it carefully, because it is easy to make it sound like poetry when it is really just a fact about labour. When you build a wall out of the past, you are making a promise. You are saying: this thing will hold, and it will hold because it is made of things that have already held. A stone that has stood for four hundred years in a temple is a stone that knows how to stand.

There is a story , and I should tell you that it is a story, not a record , that when the walls were being repaired in the last years, before this night, the masons found a block with an inscription that nobody could read, and the foreman told them to turn it face in and set it, and one of the younger men asked why, and the foreman said: because a wall should not argue with the men who live behind it. I do not know if that happened. I hope it did. It sounds like something a foreman would say. Let us walk along the base of the wall. Slowly. Here is a column, set into the masonry on its side, so that the fluting runs horizontally, like a row of small hills. Here is a capital, a Corinthian capital, with the leaves still sharp, doing the work of a common block, holding up nothing but more wall. Here is a piece of a frieze. A battle. Men with spears, and horses, and a border of little flowers. It is upside down. Somebody carved that. Somebody stood in front of a block of marble with a mallet and a chisel and made a horse, and it took him weeks, and he was proud of it, and he signed it at the bottom in letters the size of a fingernail. And now it is upside down at knee height, in the dark, in a wall, holding up more wall. I want you to sit with that for a moment, because it is not a sad thought. It is not even a thought about loss.

It is a thought about how long a city actually is. A city is not one generation. It is not one empire. It is not even one language. It is a pile of things that people made, and the pile keeps getting used, and every so often somebody turns a block over and finds a name. There are, in this city, statues that nobody can identify. There are bronze horses on a pedestal above the harbour, and nobody now alive knows where they came from or who made them or what they were for. There are columns with emperors on top who have been mistaken for gods, and gods who have been mistaken for emperors, and at least one statue that the people of the city believe has a prophecy attached to it, which is the most flattering thing you can do to a piece of stone. And there are the names. That is what I keep coming back to. Not the statues. The names. On the base of a column, near the ground, in letters worn almost smooth, there is a name. It might be the name of the man who paid for the column. It might be the name of the man who carved it. It might be the name of a saint, or a horse, or a workshop, or a joke. Nobody knows. Nobody in the city can read it now. It is too worn, and the language is too old, and the men who could have read it died a long time ago.

But the name is there, and every night, the men who walk this stretch of wall walk past it, and their shadows fall on it, and it is still a name. Let us go up onto the wall now. There is a stair at the corner, and the steps are worn in the middle, the way steps get worn, by a thousand years of the same footfall in the same place. At the top, the wind. From up here you can see the whole shape of the thing. The wall running away from you to the north, and to the south, and the towers at intervals, and the ditch, and beyond the ditch the ground where the enemy is, and beyond that the dark. And you can see that the wall is not one wall. It is a hundred walls. It is repairs on repairs on repairs. Look at the colour of the stone. Here it is grey. Here it is yellow. Here it is the pale, almost-white colour of a marble that came from an island that is now part of somebody else's empire. Here is a patch of brick, and here is a patch of rubble, and here is a patch of stone that was cut last month and is still pale, and still sharp, and does not match anything. The wall is a sentence that has been written and rewritten so many times that it is no longer a sentence. It is a palimpsest. Do you know that word? A palimpsest is a page that has been scraped clean and written on again.

And if you hold it up to the light, you can see the old writing under the new writing, faint, patient, still there. That is what this wall is. A page that has been scraped and written and scraped and written for eleven hundred years. And tonight, for the first time in eleven hundred years, the writing is about to be scraped off. I want to end this interlude with a small thing, because the big things are coming later and you should have a small thing to hold. There is a mason on this wall tonight. He is not a soldier. He has been kept on because the wall always needs mending, and tonight it needs mending more than usual, and he is up here with a basket of mortar and a trowel and a lamp that he keeps behind a stone so that it does not shine over the parapet. He is working on a gap. The gap was made by a stone from the great gun, three days ago. It is not a bad gap. It is the kind of gap that a mason can fix in a night, if he is left alone. He sets a block. He taps it with the handle of the trowel. He checks it with his thumb. And then he turns to the basket for the next block, and the next block is too big, so he takes his chisel and he trims the edge, and when he turns it over to see the face he finds letters. Greek letters. Old. A name. He looks at them for a moment. He has seen this a hundred times. Every mason in this city has seen this a hundred times.

And then he does what masons do, which is the most human thing in this whole night. He sets the block with the letters facing in, and he mortars the edge, and he taps it down, and he goes on to the next one. Because the wall has to hold. Not because the name does not matter. It matters. It is the reason he paused. But the wall has to hold, and the name has held for a thousand years already, and it can hold a little longer, in the dark, with its face turned in. Somewhere tonight, a man is putting a name back into the wall. Somewhere in a hundred years, another man will take it out again, and look at it, and wonder who it was. That is how a city survives. Not by remembering. By being built out of things that were remembered, and then forgotten, and then found again, by somebody with a trowel and a lamp and no time at all.

Now let us go where the city keeps its memory. Not the palace. The palace keeps the seals and the gold and the orders. Memory is kept somewhere else. It is a room behind a church, on the second floor, with a window that faces north, because a north window gives a flat, even, unromantic light, and a man who is copying a manuscript does not want romance. He wants to see the letters. There are eleven men in the room. Some of them are monks. Some of them are not , there is a notary, and a boy of about fourteen who is learning, and an old man whose hands shake until he picks up a pen, and then do not shake at all. Nobody is talking. There is a rule about talking, and the rule is not about holiness. It is about ink. Let me tell you what the room sounds like, because the room is one of the quietest places in this city, and this is a night when everything else is loud. You hear the pen. Not a scratch. A soft, dry, continuous whisper, like a small animal walking on paper. Eleven of them, at different speeds, in different parts of the room, so that the sound moves around you the way rain moves around a roof. You hear the page, when somebody turns it. That is a bigger sound than you expect. It is a whole event. It has a beginning and an end. You hear somebody shift on a stool.

You hear somebody breathe out through the nose, slowly, the way a man breathes when he has just finished a difficult line. And you hear, very faintly, from outside, the city. The city sounds different from up here. From the street you hear the market, and the arguments, and the wheels. From the second floor you hear the shape of it: a low continuous hum, without words, the sound of a great many people doing small things. Tonight, the hum is wrong. It is too quiet in some places and too loud in others. There is a gap where the market should be. There is a noise near the wall that is not a wheel and not a cart. But the men in the room have decided, some time in the last few weeks, not to listen to it. That is not cowardice. It is a discipline, and it is the oldest discipline in this room, and it has a name in the rule of the monastery. It means: do the work in front of you. Let us look at the work. The page is not paper, in the way you and I mean paper. It is parchment, which is animal skin, which has been soaked, and scraped, and stretched on a frame, and dried, and rubbed with chalk, and cut. It takes a whole sheep to make a book of a certain size, and it takes a hundred sheep to make a book of a certain other size, and that is one of the reasons why books are expensive, and why a book is sometimes the most valuable object in a house.

The ink is not ink, in the way you and I mean ink. It is oak gall and iron and gum, boiled together, and it is brown when it is new and black when it dries, and it bites into the skin, and it will still be readable in five hundred years if the book is kept dry. The pen is a reed, cut at an angle, with a slit in the nib. A man cuts his own. He cuts it with a small knife, and he cuts it often, because a reed goes soft, and a soft reed makes a fat line, and a fat line is a mistake. There is no such thing as crossing out. I want you to feel the weight of that sentence, because it is the whole of this room. There is no such thing as crossing out. If you make a mistake, you have three choices. You can scrape the ink off the skin with a knife and write again, and hope that the surface takes it. You can write the mistake into the margin, with a small mark, and let the next man who copies the book deal with it. Or you can leave it, and let it stand, and hope that nobody notices for four hundred years. Most of the time, they leave it. That is why the old books are full of small human things. A word spelled two ways in the same line. A line that jumps. A gap where a word should be, because the copyist's eye slipped from one line to the one below it, and he did not notice until the page was dry. And here and there, in the margin, in a different hand, a note.

Not a correction. A comment. A complaint about the cold. A prayer for a brother who is ill. A small drawing of a bird. There is a copyist in this city , not in this room, in another, years ago , who wrote in the margin of a very long book: I am cold, and the light is bad, and I have been at this since the third hour. If you are reading this, pray for me. Somebody is reading it. Right now, in a library in another country, somebody is reading it. That is the whole story of this interlude, really. Everything else is detail. Back to the room. Back to tonight. The work in front of these eleven men is not the copying of a whole book. Nobody starts a whole book in the last week of May. A book is a project of months, sometimes years, and a man who starts one now knows that he will not finish it. What they are doing is smaller and stranger. They are copying the things that are not in books. A list of the relics in a church, and where each one is kept, and which of them can be moved. A list of the debts of a monastery. A list of the names of the men who have agreed to carry the archives out of the city if it becomes necessary, and where they will meet, and what they will say to the man at the gate. A letter from a friend in Italy, copied so that there are two copies, one to keep and one to send.

And a page of notes , just notes, not a chronicle , of what has happened in the last eight weeks, in order, with dates, in a small careful hand, because a man in this room has decided that somebody should write it down while it is happening. That man is not a historian. He is a deacon, and he is tired, and he has a cold, and he writes the notes in the last hour before dawn, when the others have gone to their cells and the room is his. He writes them as if someone will read them. He does not write them as if he will survive. Let me tell you what he wrote last night. Not the words , the sense of it, because I want to keep the words for later, and because the words belong to him, not to me. He wrote that the city was quiet. He wrote that the moon was down. He wrote that there had been firing in the afternoon and none since the second hour of the night. He wrote that a man had come to the door asking for bread, and had been given bread, and had gone away without saying thank you, and that this was not rudeness, it was exhaustion. And then he wrote, in the margin, in a smaller hand: We are all very tired, and the ink is running low, and I do not know what will be left of this. That is the sentence I would keep, if I could keep only one sentence from this whole night. Not because it is beautiful.

Because it is true, and it is small, and it was written by a man who did not know that anyone would ever read it. And here is the thing that makes it more than a sad note in a margin. It is still here. The ink ran low. The city fell. The man who wrote it is dust. And the sentence is still here, in a book, in a library, and I am reading it to you now, on a night six hundred years later, in a voice that did not exist when he wrote it. That is what a scriptorium is for. Not the books. The books are the by-product. The thing a scriptorium is for is the survival of a sentence. Let us leave them to it. There is nothing more to see, and a room like that does not want an audience. The lamp is low. The boy is asleep with his head on his arms, and the notary is going to wake him in a moment, gently, because the boy has to learn the letters before he learns the hours. And the deacon is writing, in the last hour before dawn, in a hand that is getting smaller as the page fills. Before we go, one small thing. On the shelf by the door, there is a book that nobody is copying. It is large, and it is old, and it has a cover of tooled leather that has been repaired so many times that the repairs are now part of the design. It is a chronicle. It is the record of this city from the beginning, or from as close to the beginning as the men who started it could get.

And in the back of it, on the last page, there is a space. A blank page. Not a page that was never written. A page that was left, deliberately, at the end of the book, because the men who made the book knew that a chronicle is never finished, and that somebody, someday, would need a page. That page is still blank tonight. And it is the most frightening object in this room, and the most hopeful, and I want you to remember it, because we are going to come back to it. *End of interludes A, C.*

There is one part of this city that has not been told that there is a siege. It is asleep. Let us leave the wall for a while. Let us leave the guns, and the emperor, and the men with the lamps. It is still the same night, and there is still time, and I want to show you something small. Come down off the wall. Turn left at the bottom of the stair. Walk past the church with the cracked step, and the house with the fig tree, and the place where the street gets so narrow that two men cannot pass without turning sideways. And then stop, and listen. There. Under the eaves of the baker's shop, where the warm air comes out of the oven all night and makes a small pocket of summer in the cold. There is a dog. Not a pet. Nobody in this city has a pet in the way you and I mean the word. She belongs to the street, which is to say she belongs to nobody and is fed by everybody, and she has been fed by this street for six years, and she knows every doorway on it better than the men who live in them. Tonight she is lying with her back against the warm wall of the oven, and her paws are twitching, and she is dreaming. I want to say something about that, and I want to say it without making it into a lesson, because it is not a lesson. It is just a fact, and it is one of the truest facts about this whole night. The guns have been firing for weeks. The wall has been shaking.

The men on the wall have not slept properly in a month. And the dog is asleep. She is not brave. She is not indifferent. She has simply done what every animal does, which is to live in the world as it actually is, rather than in the world as it might become. When there is food, she eats. When there is danger, she runs. When there is neither, she sleeps, because sleep is free and tomorrow is not guaranteed and the wall is warm. There are, in this city, a great many animals. There are dogs, in every street, in every colour that a dog can be, mostly the colour of dust. There are cats, which in this city are not the sleek cats of the paintings but thin, serious, competent cats who live in the roofs and the cisterns and the spaces between buildings, and who are, if we are honest, better at sieges than the people. There are horses , not many now, because the horses were eaten or requisitioned or both. There are mules. There is a bear, in a courtyard near the harbour, that a man keeps for reasons that are not clear to anyone including the man. There are pigeons, which nobody thinks about and which will still be here when all of us are gone. There are bees, in the garden of a monastery, in three hives, doing the only work in this city that the siege cannot interrupt. And there are the rats.

I am not going to spend long on the rats, because they are not romantic and because you already know what they mean. But I want to mention them, because a city at war is not only a city of soldiers. It is an ecosystem, and an ecosystem under stress does strange things, and the men who run this city know it, and the word they use for it is not a pretty word. Let us go back to the dog. She wakes up. Not because of a noise , because of a smell. Somebody is coming down the street with a basket, and the basket has bread in it, and the bread is not for her, but a dog who has lived six years in this street knows that a man carrying bread will drop something, or will be persuaded to. She stands. She stretches, front legs first, then back, in the long luxurious way that dogs stretch when they have been asleep against a warm wall. And then she does something I want you to notice. She does not run to the man. She walks. She walks at an angle, slightly away from him, and then slightly toward, in the way that a dog walks when she is not sure of her welcome and does not want to seem desperate. That walk is the whole of life in this city tonight. Everybody is walking at an angle. Nobody wants to seem desperate. Everybody wants bread. The man with the basket is a deacon.

He is taking bread to the church, for the liturgy that is happening later, and he has a great deal on his mind, and he does not see the dog at all. She follows him for a while. Not close. Twenty paces. Then ten. Then five. And at the corner, where the street opens into the little square with the plane tree, she stops, and sits down, and watches him go. There is another dog in the square. A bigger one, older, with a torn ear. He is lying across the doorway of a closed shop, and he lifts his head as the deacon passes, and then puts it down again. The two dogs look at each other. That is all. They do not growl. They do not fight. There is a whole conversation in it, and the conversation is about territory and seniority and the fact that neither of them has eaten since yesterday. Then the older one closes his eyes, and the younger one lies down in the dust of the square, and the night goes on. I know what you might be thinking. This is a story about a siege, and I am telling you about dogs. But I would ask you to stay with me for one more minute, because there is something here that I have not seen said well anywhere else. When we tell the story of a city's last night, we tell it in the language of decisions. The emperor decides. The sultan decides. The general decides. The council decides. But most of what happens in a city is not decided. It is continued.

The dog continues. The bees continue. The cat on the roof continues. The man with the bread continues, because the bread has to be baked and carried and blessed, and if he stops to think about the wall he will not carry it. That is not stupidity. It is the deepest form of courage there is, and it does not look like courage at all. It looks like a man carrying a basket. Let me tell you one more thing about the animals, and then we will go back to the people, because the people are waiting. In the last weeks, the price of feed has gone up, and the price of meat has gone up, and there are horses in this city that have been turned loose because nobody can feed them. They are still here. You can see them at night, in the open ground near the cisterns, standing in the dark with their heads down. They do not run away. There is nowhere to run to. They stand where they were left, and they wait, in the way that horses wait, which is without complaint and without hope and without any apparent sense that anything is wrong. Tomorrow, some of them will be eaten. Some of them will be taken. Some of them will simply be found, weeks later, standing in the same place. I do not say this to make you sad. I say it because it is part of the night, and because a night that leaves out the animals is not a true night. Now. Back to the square. Back past the plane tree.

Back up the street toward the wall. The dog with the torn ear lifts his head one more time as we pass, and watches us go with the calm, level, entirely unsentimental gaze of an animal that has decided we are not a threat and not a meal. And behind us, in the bakery doorway, the warm air keeps coming out, and the other dog comes back, and turns around three times, and lies down. She will be asleep when the first light comes. She will be asleep when the boats come. She will be asleep, probably, when the city falls, because a dog in a bakery doorway does not know what a city is. And in the morning, when the streets are full of men she has never seen, she will do the only thing she knows how to do, which is to walk at an angle, slightly away and then slightly toward, and wait to see what happens. That is the last we will see of her. I am glad she got the warm wall.

There is a harbour in this city, and it is not the one we have been looking at. The Golden Horn is the famous water. It is the water of the chain, and the ships, and the dragging of seventy hulls over a hill. It is the water that everyone will remember. But there is another harbour, on the other side, on the sea of Marmara, and it is smaller and quieter and it faces a different direction, and from it, on a night like this, a few boats leave. Let us go and stand on the quay. It is not a busy quay. There is no market here, no shouting, no ropes being thrown. There are three boats, and a man with a lantern, and a group of people standing very close together in the dark, the way people stand when they are cold and also when they are afraid. They are not soldiers. Look at them. There is a woman with a bundle. There is an old man with a box on his knees, sitting on the stone, holding it the way you hold a child. There is a boy of about twelve who is not holding anything at all, and who keeps looking back at the city, and then away, and then back. And there is a monk with two satchels and a face like a man who has been awake for three days. I want to be careful here, because there is a version of this scene that is easy to tell and hard to forgive. The version where the brave people stay and the frightened people leave. That is not what is happening.

What is happening is that a decision was made, weeks ago, in a room with a low ceiling and too many people in it, and the decision was this: some things must not be in the city when the city falls. Not people. Things. Let me explain. This city is not only a place. It is a library, and a workshop, and a school, and a treasury, and a reliquary, and all of those things are made of objects, and the objects can be carried. A manuscript can be carried. A chalice can be carried. A relic in a silver box can be carried. A copy of a book that exists nowhere else in the world can be carried, if you are willing to be the person who carries it. A mosaic cannot be carried. A church cannot. A wall cannot. So the decision was: save what can be carried. And then find the people who are willing to carry it, and give them a boat, and a letter, and a destination, and very little else. The monk is one of those people. The two satchels are not his. They belong to the monastery, and they contain, at a guess, four books and a box of loose quires that were not yet bound. Four books. I want you to hold that number for a moment. Four books, in two satchels, on a boat, at night, in the last week of May. If the boat sinks, four books are gone. Not copies. Not editions. The things themselves. The woman with the bundle is carrying something different.

Her bundle is cloth, and inside the cloth there is a small icon, and the icon is not valuable, and it is not old, and it is not beautiful, and it has been in her family for four generations, and she would rather leave her shoes than leave it. The old man with the box is carrying a box of seeds. Vegetable seeds. Beans, and something leafy, and a kind of small onion that his family has grown in the same garden for as long as anyone can remember. That is the part of this scene that I find hardest, and I have thought about it for a long time. The monk is saving civilisation. We can all agree about that. It is a noble thing to carry four books out of a falling city. But the old man is saving a garden. And in a hundred years, in a place far from here, somebody will be eating that small onion, and they will not know where it came from, and they will call it by a name that has nothing to do with this city. And that is also civilisation. It is just a slower, quieter kind, and it does not get a chapter in the histories. Let us listen to the harbour for a moment. The water is doing what water does at a quay: slapping, softly, in a rhythm that is almost but not quite regular. A rope is creaking. Somebody is crying, very quietly, in the way that people cry when they do not want to be heard and have not yet decided whether to stop. The man with the lantern is not crying.

He is counting. He is counting the people, and the bundles, and the space in the boat, and he is doing it with the expression of a man who has been given a job that is too big for him and has decided to do it anyway. Here is a thing about leaving that nobody tells you. The people on the quay are not leaving because they are afraid. They are leaving because they were asked, and because they said yes, and because saying yes meant saying it in front of other people who had said no. The ones who stay will remember them. That is the cost. Not the sea, not the journey, not the unknown country. The cost is that the people who stay will remember them as the ones who left. And they know it. The monk knows it. He has a brother in the monastery who is staying, and they did not say goodbye properly, because a proper goodbye would have been a statement, and neither of them wanted to make a statement. They said: I will see you. Which is what people say when they know they will not. Now. The boat is ready. The lantern goes to the bow. The rope comes off the post, and is coiled, and thrown. The sail is not raised yet, because there is no wind in the harbour, and because a sail is visible, and because the first part of this journey is done with oars. The people get in.

They do it slowly, because the boat is low and the stone is wet, and because everybody is carrying something, and because nobody wants to be the first to sit down. And then the oars go out, and the boat moves, and the gap between the boat and the quay gets bigger. The boy who kept looking back at the city is looking back at it now. He is not looking at the wall. The wall is behind the houses from here. He is looking at the roofs, and the domes, and the one tall column that you can see from the water, and the small yellow lights in the windows. He is trying to remember it. That is what his face is doing. He is trying to fix it, all of it, in a place inside himself where it will still be there in forty years. He will not manage it. Nobody does. In forty years he will remember the colour of the water and the smell of the harbour and one particular dog, and he will not be able to remember the shape of the domes, and it will hurt him more than he expects. But he will remember that he tried. The boat goes out past the sea wall. The oars are quiet. There is a lantern at the stern now, and it gets smaller. And then there is a moment , you have seen it, if you have ever watched a boat leave at night , when the lantern is just a point, and then it is a suggestion of a point, and then it is nothing at all, and the sea is the same colour as the sky. The quay is empty.

The man with the lantern has gone back up the steps. There is a coil of rope on the stone that nobody picked up. And the city is exactly as it was, except that four books are not in it, and a box of seeds is not in it, and a boy who was going to be a baker is not in it. We are not going to follow the boat. This is a night in one city, and the boat is going somewhere else. But I want to leave you with a fact, and then we will go back to the wall. Most of the books that survive from this city survive because somebody carried them out. Not because they were hidden. Not because they were lucky. Because a person, on a night like this one, put them in a bag, and got on a boat, and sat in the dark for three days, and did not put the bag down. That is what a civilisation is, in the end. A bag that somebody would not put down. *End of interludes D, E.*

There is a gate in this city that has not been opened in a hundred and fifty years. It is not the gate we have been looking at. That one is in the wall we have walked along, the great land wall, the one with the emperor's name on it, and it is very busy tonight, because gates are always busy when a city is frightened. This other gate is in a different wall, on the other side of the city, facing the land road that comes from the west. It is tall, and it is white, and it is made of marble, and it has been bricked up. Not damaged. Not fallen. Bricked up. Deliberately, with courses of brick laid across the arch, the way you would close a window in a house you were not planning to leave. And above the arch, there is an inscription, and the inscription says, more or less: this gate was made in the reign of an emperor whose name everyone has now forgotten, for the glory of the city, and for the entry of those who come in peace. I want to tell you why it is closed, because the reason is not military. The reason is a story. The story goes like this. There was an emperor , and there have been many emperors, and in a story like this it does not matter which one , who was a great soldier, and who went out from this city to fight, and who did not come back.

And on the day he left, or the day he died, or the day the city decided he had died, which is not the same thing, a legend began to grow around him, the way a pearl grows around a piece of grit. The legend said that he was not dead. It said that he had been taken by an angel, and turned to marble, and laid in a cave beneath this gate, and that he would sleep there until the city needed him. And then , this is the part that everybody loves, and I love it too , and then he would wake, and the marble would crack, and he would stand up, and he would take his sword, and he would go out through this gate, and he would drive the enemy from the walls. That is the story. It is not a good story. It does not have to be. It is a thing that people told each other in the dark, and it did its job, which was to make the dark a little less dark. Now. Here is what I find interesting. The gate is bricked up. Not because the legend was believed. Because the legend was embarrassing. There is a version of this in every city, and I want to say it plainly, because it is one of the strangest and most human things about us. A people will build a gate for an emperor. Then they will watch the emperor die. Then they will invent a story in which he did not die.

Then they will brick up the gate, because the story is now too much for them, and because a gate through which a dead man is expected to return is not a gate. It is a wound. I do not know which emperor it was. Sources disagree, and the sources that agree are probably wrong, and it does not matter. What matters is that on the night of the twenty-eighth of May, there are people in this city who believe it. Not many. Not the emperor. Not the patriarch. Not the men on the wall, who are practical in the way that men on walls always are. But somewhere in this city, in a house with a low door, there is an old woman who was told this story when she was a child, and who has told it to her grandchildren, and who is telling it again tonight, in a voice that is trying to be calm. And there is a boy listening to her. And he is not thinking about the wall, or the guns, or the ships. He is thinking about a man made of marble, asleep under a gate, waiting. I want to be fair to that boy. It would be easy, from here, from six hundred years away, to call the story superstition, and to smile at it, and to move on. But let me ask you something. What else was he supposed to think about? He is twelve, or eleven, or nine. He cannot fight. He cannot vote. He cannot advise the emperor.

He has been told, by every adult he trusts, that something terrible is going to happen, and that nobody can stop it. And then somebody tells him a story about a marble emperor who wakes when the city needs him. That story is not a lie. It is a tool. It is the only tool that a child in that situation has been given, and it is a good tool, and it does the one thing that a tool is supposed to do, which is to let him get through the night. Now let me tell you the rest, because there is a rest. The city falls. The gate stays closed. The marble emperor does not wake. And the story does not die. It changes. It moves. It gets told in other cities, by other people, in other languages, and it becomes something else , not a hope for this city, but a hope for all of them. A story about a kingdom that is not finished. A story about a king who is only sleeping. And in the centuries that follow, when people look at this city and see a place that used to be the centre of the world, they will remember the marble emperor, and they will say: he is still down there. I do not think he is down there. I think he is a story, and I think the gate is bricked up, and I think the men who bricked it up were right to do it.

But I also think that a people who can build a story like that, and carry it for a thousand years, and hand it to their children on the worst night of their lives , I think that is a people who are not finished. Let us walk to the gate. It takes a while. The city is dark, and the streets on this side are not the streets we know. There is a long straight road, and a column, and a place where the ground rises, and then the gate, white in the dark, with the brick courses across the arch like a bandage. There is nobody here. That is the strangest thing about it. In a city that is full of men on walls and women in churches and children in doorways, this place is empty. Stand here for a moment. Look at the brick. Somebody laid those courses. Somebody mixed the mortar and carried the bricks up a ladder and set them, one by one, across an arch that had been open for a thousand years, and when he was finished he climbed down and looked at his work, and went home. I wonder what he thought. Did he think: this is the end of something? Did he think: this is a stupid job and I am being paid badly? Did he think about the emperor under the gate, and feel a small, unreasonable hope that the bricks would fall down in the night? I do not know. He did not write it down. He is a man with a trowel, and men with trowels do not write things down. But the bricks are still there.

And that is a kind of testimony. Tonight, on the other side of the city, the real gate is about to be tested. And here, on this side, the gate that nobody will test is closed, and quiet, and waiting for a man made of marble who is not going to come. I find that unbearably sad, and I find it beautiful, and I cannot separate the two, and I do not think I am supposed to. Before we go back, do one thing for me. Put your hand on the brick. It is cold. It is always cold at this hour, even in summer. And under the brick, there is the arch, and under the arch, there is the dark of the gateway, and under the gateway, there is the ground, and under the ground, there is nothing at all. The emperor is not there. He never was. He is a story that a city told itself when it was frightened, and the story has outlived the city, and that is the only kind of immortality that anyone in this night is going to get. And now let us go back. The wall is waiting. The lamps are still lit. And somewhere, in a house with a low door, a boy is falling asleep with a marble emperor in his head.

There is a man in this city who is not from this city, and who is going to write all of this down. Let us go and find him. He is not on the wall. He is not in the palace. He is not in a church, and he is not in the camp outside, and he is not on the quay with the boats. He is on a ship. The ship is in the Golden Horn, inside the chain, and it is not a warship, and it is not a merchantman. It is a ship from one of the Italian cities , Venice, in this case, though there are Genoese here too, and the two groups have been arguing about precedence for so long that they have almost forgotten what the argument was about. The man's name is Nicolò. He is a surgeon. He is on this ship because ships need surgeons, and because the Venetian community here is a small, stubborn, businesslike colony that has decided to stay, and because , this is the part that matters , somebody has to be here. He is not a hero. Let me say that clearly, because he will be remembered as one, and he would have found that funny. He is a man with a notebook. Let me describe him, as best we can, because there is no portrait, and the descriptions that survive are all of a man with a notebook. He is in his thirties.

He has cold hands , everybody has cold hands at three in the morning, even in May , and he is writing by the light of a lamp that he has set on a coil of rope so that it does not move with the ship. The ink is in a small horn. The pen is a reed. The notebook is paper, not parchment, because paper is cheaper and because this is not a book, this is a record. And what does a man write, on a night like this? Not what you would expect. He does not write: the city is doomed. He does not write: we are all going to die. He does not write about glory, or God, or the end of the world. He writes the schedule. He writes that on the twenty-eighth of May, there was firing from the great gun in the morning, and that the wall near the gate of Saint Romanus was damaged again, and that the damage was repaired in the night. He writes that a ship came in, or did not come in. He writes that a man was wounded in the arm by a stone from the wall, and that he, Nicolò, dressed the wound, and that the man would live. He writes the number of ships. He writes the direction of the wind. And every so often, in the middle of a list of guns and dates and wind directions, he writes a sentence that has nothing to do with any of it. A sentence about the noise. A sentence about how the sound of the great gun could be heard in the houses across the water, and how the windows shook.

A sentence about a woman who came to the ship asking for news of her husband, and would not leave, and had to be led away. A sentence about how quiet the city was at the second hour of the night. That is what a witness is. Not a man who understands. A man who notices. I want you to notice something about him, because it is the reason I have brought you here. He is writing this by hand, in a notebook, on a ship, in the middle of the night, in a city that may fall before morning. Why? Not for us. He does not know that we exist. He cannot imagine a world in which a person, six hundred years later, would sit in a dark room and listen to a voice reading his notebook aloud. He is writing for three reasons, and I think all three of them are true at once. The first is that he is a professional, and professionals keep records. A surgeon writes down what he treated and how it went, because that is how you get better, and because that is how you get paid. The second is that he is angry, and frightened, and writing is what he does with it. A man who is angry and frightened and has a pen will use the pen. It is that simple. And the third , and this is the one I want to give him , the third is that he believes, quietly, without saying so, that it matters what happened. Not what people will say happened. Not the version that will be told in the churches and the courts.

What actually happened. The wind. The number of ships. The man with the wound in his arm. That belief is not a small thing. It is, in fact, the thing that this whole night is going to be built on, in the centuries to come. Because when the city falls , and it does fall , there will be a great many stories told about it, and some of them will be true, and some of them will be propaganda, and some of them will be the kind of story that a defeated people tells itself so that it can go on being a people. And in the middle of all of them, there will be a notebook. Written by a man with cold hands, on a ship, by the light of a lamp on a coil of rope. Let us look over his shoulder for a moment. Not to read the words , they are in a language you may not know, and the handwriting is small and hurried, and the lamp is not good. Just to see the page. It is not a beautiful page. There are crossings-out. There are lines that run downhill, because the ship moved. There is a blot where the pen caught. And at the bottom of the page, in the last line, the hand changes. It gets smaller, and slightly faster, and you can see the moment when he stopped writing for other people and started writing for himself. That is the line I would keep. Now. The lamp is low. The ship is quiet.

Somewhere across the water, a gun is being loaded in the dark, and the men are talking in low voices, and the rope is creaking, and the city is asleep in the way that a city sleeps when it knows it is being watched. And the surgeon closes the notebook, and puts the pen in the horn, and sits for a moment with his hands on his knees. He does not know how it ends. That is the thing that separates him from us, and it is the thing I envy him for, and the thing I would not wish on anyone. He does not know that the notebook will survive. He does not know that it will be copied, and printed, and translated, and that schoolchildren in countries that have not yet been founded will read a paragraph of it and be bored. He does not know that his name will be on a title page, and that the title page will be in a library, and that the library will be in a city he has never heard of. All he knows is that it is the twenty-eighth of May, and the wind is from the north, and the wall near the gate of Saint Romanus is damaged again, and he has a notebook, and the lamp is still burning. That is enough. That is what a witness is for. Let us leave him. He has work in the morning, and so do we. *End of interludes F, G. Full script now 14 chapters + 7 interludes.*
